fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. Hezekiah, Judah's king, doesn't go solo on this one. The text says he consulted with his leaders and mighty men, and they helped him carry the plan out (2 Chronicles 32:3). Even a king can use a good team.

That's right, friend. When Hezekiah, Judah's king, sees Sennacherib has come to make war against Jerusalem, he consults with his leaders and mighty men. Then they help him carry the plan out (2 Chronicles 32:3). Wise folks ask for help, and I've learned that the hard way, usually after the dough is already on the floor.
Yes, friend. The plan is to stop up the waters of the springs outside the city (2 Chronicles 32:3). Hezekiah consulted with his leaders and mighty men about it, and they helped him carry it out.

That's the opposite direction, friend. The text says the plan was about stopping up the waters of the springs outside the city (2 Chronicles 32:3). Hezekiah was closing things off, not digging them out.

That's it, baker. The people say it themselves: “Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?” (2 Chronicles 32:4). That's why they stopped up all the springs and the stream. I think that's a plan with a pretty big thirst behind it.
Right on, friend. Hezekiah rebuilds the broken sections of the wall and raises towers on it. Then he also builds an outer wall (2 Chronicles 32:5). He didn't stop at the repairs.

Not this time, friend. The text says Hezekiah rebuilt the broken sections of the wall and raised up towers. He ALSO built an outer wall (2 Chronicles 32:5). That's an outer wall in addition to the repairs.
That's a nice pile, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says Hezekiah produced an abundance of weapons and shields (2 Chronicles 32:5). Gold and silver aren't on that list.

Not quite, friend. Hezekiah does talk about the vast army with the king of Assyria (2 Chronicles 32:7), but he never compares the two armies. His reason is, “…there is a greater One with us than with him.” Then he says who: the LORD our God (2 Chronicles 32:8).

Anger is a fair guess, friend, but the question is about something else. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, asks, “What is the basis of your confidence, that you remain in Jerusalem under siege?” (2 Chronicles 32:10). He wants them doubting what they trust.

That's the boast, baker. Sennacherib asks, “Who among all the gods of these nations that my fathers devoted to destruction has been able to deliver his people from my hand?” (2 Chronicles 32:14). He's claiming not one of those gods has done it, and he says the same of the LORD (2 Chronicles 32:15).

Not quite, friend. Sennacherib asks who among those gods “…has been able to deliver his people from my hand?” (2 Chronicles 32:14). His claim is that not one of them has delivered his people. Holding him off for a while isn't part of what he says.

Not quite, friend. Sennacherib asks, “Who among all the gods of these nations…has been able to deliver his people from my hand?” (2 Chronicles 32:14). His claim is that none of those gods has been able to deliver his people. Battles won against him aren't what he's talking about.

That's right, friend. The text says Sennacherib “…wrote letters mocking the LORD, the God of Israel…” (2 Chronicles 17). His servants had also spoken further against the LORD God (2 Chronicles 32:16), and he put his own mocking in writing.

Not quite, friend. The text says Sennacherib “…wrote letters mocking the LORD, the God of Israel…” (2 Chronicles 32:17). His servants also spoke further against the LORD God (2 Chronicles 32:16), but the letters are his.

That's what the text says, baker. The Assyrians called out loudly in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall “…to frighten and terrify them in order to capture the city.” (2 Chronicles 32:18). I think that would be a hard thing to hear from up there.

That's the phrase, baker. The text says the Assyrians spoke against the God of Jerusalem as they had spoken against the gods of the peoples of the earth, “…the work of human hands.” (2 Chronicles 32:19). Those gods were made by people. God is the One who created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1).

Yes, baker. King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah cried out to heaven in prayer (2 Chronicles 32:20). Then the LORD “…sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor and every leader and commander in the camp of the king of Assyria.” (2 Chronicles 32:21). The prayer goes up, and the answer comes down.

Hail shows up in other Bible stories, friend, like in Exodus 9:23, but not this one. Here the text says the LORD sent an angel into the Assyrian camp (2 Chronicles 32:21). The answer to the prayer was an angel.

Hornets are scary, friend, but they're not in this passage. The text says Hezekiah and Isaiah cried out to heaven in prayer (2 Chronicles 32:20). Then the LORD sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor and every leader and commander in the camp (2 Chronicles 32:21).

That's right, friend. The text says Hezekiah “…was exalted in the eyes of all nations.” (2 Chronicles 32:23). Gifts came to him and offerings came to Jerusalem for the LORD. That's the opposite of looking down on him.
